common_name: Dark Vader Pulmonaria (Deep Violet-Blue Silver-Spotted Lungwort)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring or fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Dark Vader bears unusually dark violet-blue flowers over heavily silvered leaves.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; good drainage combined with consistent moisture keeps the fleshy roots from rotting while preventing the leaves from scorching in a dry site. Dark Vader produces unusually deep violet-blue flowers, darker and more saturated than most lungwort cultivars, opening in early spring atop leaves that are heavily overlaid with silver spotting, giving the foliage striking presence well after the flowers fade for the rest of the season. Like other pulmonaria, it thrives in the moist, dappled shade of a woodland setting and pairs well with hostas, ferns, and other spring-flowering shade perennials such as hellebores and epimedium. Cut back tattered foliage after flowering if powdery mildew appears in humid summer weather, and divide congested clumps every three to four years in fall or early spring.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring or fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Milky Way carries an especially dense scattering of silver spots across the leaf surface, giving a starry, night-sky effect.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; consistent moisture and good drainage together keep the fleshy roots healthy while preventing leaf scorch in drier sites. Milky Way bears a dense, uniform scattering of small silver spots across its green leaves, evoking a starry night sky, with clusters of pink buds opening to blue flowers in early spring that provide welcome color before most other shade perennials emerge. The richly spotted foliage remains attractive through the growing season, making it a strong textural and color companion to hostas, ferns, and other woodland shade plants. Cut back foliage after flowering if powdery mildew develops in humid summer weather, encouraging fresh new growth, and divide congested clumps every three to four years in fall or early spring.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Orion bears unusually large flowers for a hardy geranium and blooms over a long season with occasional shearing.

directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade, with afternoon shade appreciated in hot climates. Orion produces exceptionally large, vivid violet-blue flowers with a small white center, bigger than most hardy geranium cultivars, held above a vigorous, mounding clump of deeply cut foliage that blooms heavily from late spring into summer. Its strong color and generous flower size make it a standout in the perennial border, and shearing the plant back by half after the first flush of bloom fades encourages a tidy regrowth of foliage and a good second round of flowers later in the season. It tolerates heat and some drought once established, though consistent moisture supports the longest bloom period, and dividing congested clumps every three to four years in spring keeps the plant vigorous.

common_name: Brookside Hardy Geranium (Clear Blue Finely Cut Cranesbill)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Brookside bears very finely dissected, almost fern-like foliage and clear sky-blue flowers over a long summer season.

directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade, with afternoon shade appreciated in hot climates. Brookside produces clear, true sky-blue flowers with a small white eye over finely cut, almost lacy, fern-like foliage that gives the whole plant a soft, airy texture different from the coarser leaves of many hardy geranium cultivars. It flowers over a long season from late spring into summer, with a light shearing after the first flush encouraging repeat bloom and fresh foliage. Its billowing, slightly sprawling habit works well tumbling over the edge of a border or path, and it combines nicely with yellow- or chartreuse-foliaged companions for color contrast. It tolerates heat and some drought once established, and dividing congested clumps every three to four years in spring keeps the plant vigorous.

common_name: Ann Folkard Hardy Geranium (Magenta Black-Eyed Trailing Cranesbill)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Ann Folkard has an unusually sprawling, trailing habit compared to most mounding hardy geranium cultivars, useful for scrambling through companion plants.

directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade, with afternoon shade appreciated in hot climates. Ann Folkard is a distinctive hardy geranium with a long, sprawling, trailing habit rather than the tidy mound of most cultivars, sending out long stems that scramble through and over neighboring plants, studded with vivid magenta flowers marked by a bold black center from late spring through summer. Its foliage emerges chartreuse-yellow in spring, especially in a sunnier position, gradually greening as the season progresses, adding a second layer of color interest beyond the flowers. Its scrambling habit makes it useful for weaving through shrub borders or draping over a wall, though it can be cut back hard if it spreads further than wanted. Divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring to maintain vigor.
